Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-29 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Liam Carter (Redwood AE), Sofia Nguyen (Redwood SE), Amir Rahman (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (Aurelia Head of ML), Carlos Duarte (Aurelia Platform Eng), Evan Shaw (Aurelia SRE), Marta Ruiz (Aurelia Product)

Summary (auto): weekly pilot check-in. Main focus microburst hedging and TTFT. Agreed to run a 10k request hedging test and share kernel decision spreadsheet.

[00:00] Liam (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda: run through the latest latency runs, triage the microburst tails, confirm a hedging test, then next steps. this is a relatively short one so we'll try to stay tight.

[00:22] Priya (Aurelia): thanks liam. yeah we had a few late tickets from the SRE team hitting big spikes yesterday so wanted to get your read. we ran your last patch with prefix cache on — saw some improvement but the very long tails linger.

[01:05] Sofia (Redwood): quick context — we pushed a soft enable of prefix/K V cache and changed the batching policy to smaller windows for short seqs. that reduced median ttft by about 12% but the 99.9 still had microbursts. some of that looks like kernel handoff for longer contexts.

[01:48] Carlos (Aurelia): log note — our typical sequence length 98% under 64 tokens but a non-trivial tail to 512 from summarization workflows. so when the batching window hits those, it changes the kernel path.

[02:20] Amir (Redwood): mhm, that kernel-path flip is where we saw jittered latency. switching kernels mid-stream can create a microsecond wall but in practice those blocks become milliseconds. we think hedging — firing a lightweight fallback path for the very first token — helps.

[03:02] Evan (Aurelia): can you define hedging? we saw that term but not totally sure the mechanisms.

[03:22] Sofia (Redwood): sure. hedging here means sending a very small, conservative exec to a low-latency kernel variant (quantized tiny) in parallel with the full execution, but cancel the slower one if the fast one wins. for us that's usually a 4-bit quantized kernel optimized for short sequences. it's essentially an optimistic fastpath.

[04:00] Marta (Aurelia): sounds a bit risky data-quality wise. will the hedged output degrade text quality?

[04:18] Liam (Redwood): good question. hedging is only for the first token/time-to-first-token; quality delta is minimal for many systems because the heavy decoding happens after. for our tests we compare token-level distribution — the fastpath matches baseline in >95% of cases for your summarization prompt family.

[04:50] Priya (Aurelia): interesting. what about streaming handshake overhead — we noticed streaming setups introduced some extra bytes on the wire and handshakes that shift the timing.

[05:15] Sofia (Redwood): yep, streaming handshake can add 40–70ms depending on client setup. we recommended persistent connections and early negotiation. also our runtime supports a streaming warm handshake to prime the kv cache which helps. sometimes the transcript or the logs show it as "streaming hand shank" in the traces — sorry firefly transcription quirk.

[06:05] Carlos (Aurelia): side note: we run a proxy that sometimes buffers chunks, that might amplify microburst effect.

[06:28] Amir (Redwood): ok quick show of numbers — last run (10/27) median ttft = 82ms, p95 = 210ms, p99 = 640ms, p99.9 = 1.8s. with prefix cache on median down to 72ms, p95 190ms, but p99.9 still around 1.6s. hedging candidate dropped p99.9 to ~420ms in our bench harness against the curated prompt set.

[07:15] Priya (Aurelia): that's promising. are we seeing any incorrect cancels — like both the fast and slow path returning and your system double-counting?

[07:34] Sofia (Redwood): we added idempotent request tags and a lightweight cancel token. sometimes the cancel races and traces show the slow path finishing but we ignore it. there's a small metric noise but not functional duplication. we'll share traces.

[08:05] Evan (Aurelia): do you need to change our dedicated config or can this run on hosted? our security profile prefers dedicated for PHI in some flows.

[08:25] Liam (Redwood): hedging is runtime-level; it can run on Hosted or Dedicated but the kernel variants available depend on the infra. on your Dedicated pool we can pin the quantized kernels and validate through the reserved nodes. for Hosted we have the short-seq fastpath but fewer custom kernel flavors.

[09:05] Carlos (Aurelia): kernel choices — we noticed auto-selection sometimes prefers an attention kernel tuned for long seqs even when the request is short, because of historical metrics. can we force per-route kernel bind?

[09:35] Amir (Redwood): yes per-route kernel binds are possible. our recommendation is to use a small ruleset: if incoming seq median < 128 then prefer fastpath kernel A; if >256 prefer kernel B; default to heuristics for mixed. we can surface that in the console.

[10:00] Priya (Aurelia): what about quantization artifacts for clinical content — do we have a quality regression suite?

[10:20] Sofia (Redwood): we do integrated evals — token-level KL, BLEU-ish measures, plus a set of safety/regression prompts. for the hedging fastpath the mismatch on your summarization set was within acceptable thresholds. we'll attach the eval report.

[11:05] Liam (Redwood): wanted to call out an oddity in one of your tail traces — looks like a GC pause on the client proxy around 03:14:22 which lines up with a 600ms spike. might not be server-side.

[11:32] Carlos (Aurelia): yep our node pool has occasional GC churn when memory fragmentation spikes. we'll check.

[12:05] Marta (Aurelia): ok can we talk hedging test design? what does the 10k job look like?

[12:22] Sofia (Redwood): we'll run 10k requests sampled from your production prompt distribution with realistic concurrency (we recommend 50 concurrent) and measure TTFT tails, cancellation rates, and quality delta. we'll run baseline, prefix cache enabled, and hedging enabled. expectation: hedging reduces 99.9 by >60% with <5% quality delta on first-token alignment.

[13:05] Priya (Aurelia): how do we validate aborts? sometimes canceled slow paths produce logs that look like errors at the app layer.

[13:24] Amir (Redwood): use unique request IDs, we return a cancel flag in the response metadata so you can filter. we'll provide a script to post-process your logs matching by request ID.

[14:00] Evan (Aurelia): what about security/compliance — any change for SOC2 or logging retention with hedging?

[14:18] Liam (Redwood): no change to audit logs. hedging just changes runtime selection. for Private/Dedicated deployments we keep all audit artifacts in your VPC. we'll still need your SOC2 checklist signoff for Dedicated.

[15:05] Carlos (Aurelia): curious: did you compare hedging vs just lowering batching window for short-seq traffic?

[15:28] Sofia (Redwood): yes we ran an ablation. dropping batching window from 20ms to 5ms reduces median but increases cost and throughput overhead; hedging is cheaper because it targets only the first token and keeps larger batches for full decode. hedging + small window produced best tails with moderate cost increase.

[16:10] Priya (Aurelia): cost numbers? we need ballpark for pilot budgeting.

[16:30] Amir (Redwood): rough: hedging added ~7% CPU/GPU cycles in bench but reduced end-user P99 SLA breaches which in your domain equates to fewer failovers. we can quantify with your actual request mix — we'll run a cost simulation.

[17:05] Marta (Aurelia): also important: can this be A/Bed to a subset of users? we want to start with non-critical tenants.

[17:22] Liam (Redwood): yes, canary/A-B via route tags in the console. we can do 5% traffic for 24h and observe metrics and roll back instantly.

[18:00] Carlos (Aurelia): timeline — if we get sequence-length CSV today, how fast can you run the hedging test?

[18:14] Sofia (Redwood): once we have the CSV and sample prompts, we can prepare the bench harness in 24h and run the 10k in ~2 hours; analysis another day. realistically results by Monday EOD.

[18:45] Priya (Aurelia): that works. one more question: do you support per-tenant kernel preferences for multi-tenant flows? we may want to opt certain customers into the hedging fastpath.

[19:05] Amir (Redwood): yes per-tenant rules are supported via route configuration; on Dedicated it's trivial, on Hosted we may need a small feature flag but it's on our roadmap and we can enable for your account.

[19:40] Liam (Redwood): quick demo snippet — (screen share audio) here is the console view of kernel binds and the hedging toggle. note the metric panel showing p99.9 before and after. sorry the at times the screen capture text says "hedge enable" as "edge enable" because of encoding.

[22:30] (screen quiet, ambient typing)

[23:10] Priya (Aurelia): looking at the dashboard — I see a big delta in one bucket labeled "summarizer-512". does that mean some requests got misclassified?

[23:32] Sofia (Redwood): likely the router used historical routing. we can force-classify by tag or by a short-seq heuristic that inspects the prompt length client-side. recommended to add a client header for expected max tokens.

[24:05] Carlos (Aurelia): ok action: we'll add X-Expected-MaxToken header to our proxy and provide that CSV.

[24:28] Evan (Aurelia): small nit — when you cancel slow path, we sometimes see a warning in our logs that looks like an error. will you help tune our logging?

[24:46] Liam (Redwood): yes we'll provide guidance and a regex to filter hedging cancels from noisey alerts.

[25:20] Marta (Aurelia): are there any fallback modes if the hedging fastpath gives unacceptable quality?

[25:40] Sofia (Redwood): yes fallback policies: prefered is automatic rollback of hedging on that route if quality regressions exceed threshold, or force decode on the full kernel for flagged tenants. also can set per-route quality thresholds that trigger rollback.

[26:15] Amir (Redwood): also want to call out microburst aggregation where spikes cluster by upstream cron jobs; in those cases hedging helps but you also want smoothing at the proxy level.

[26:45] Carlos (Aurelia): we'll double-check cron alignment.

[27:20] (brief pause)

[27:40] Priya (Aurelia): ok let's lock next steps so we don't drift.

[27:50] Liam (Redwood): readout: 1) Aurelia to provide sequence-length CSV and sample prompts (Carlos) due 2026-10-31. 2) Redwood to run 10k hedging bench and share results + traces (Sofia) target 2026-11-01. 3) Redwood to upload kernel-choice spreadsheet and rationale (Liam) 2026-11-01. 4) Both to schedule canary rollout 2026-11-02 (Priya/Evan) and confirm incident playbook.

[28:30] Carlos (Aurelia): noted. also can you share your eval harness so we can run locally?

[28:46] Amir (Redwood): yes we'll package a small harness repo — lightweight script to replay prompts with request ids and capture metadata.

[29:05] Marta (Aurelia): blockers? anything we should know that might delay?

[29:22] Sofia (Redwood): only dependency is the sample prompts and header so we can route correctly. otherwise we have the infra.

[30:00] Priya (Aurelia): any competitors offering similar hedging? we briefly looked; Anthropic has some multi-path tricks but not exactly same tradeoffs.

[30:25] Liam (Redwood): yeah others have hybrid approaches. our hedging is tuned to minimize cost while cutting tails. we'll add a short note comparing approaches in the kernel spreadsheet.

[31:10] Evan (Aurelia): metrics we'll watch during canary: TTFT p99.9, request cancellation rate, first-token dist KL, and app error noise.

[31:32] Sofia (Redwood): noted — we'll configure Grafana dashboards and alert thresholds.

[32:00] (brief side conversation about scheduling)

[33:00] Priya (Aurelia): ok small operational question — for dedicated nodes, kernel upgrades require restart windows? we want minimal disruption.

[33:22] Amir (Redwood): rolling upgrades supported; kernel micro-updates are hot-pluggable in many cases. major ABI changes require node bounce but we can schedule in low-traffic hours and do drained rollouts.

[34:05] Carlos (Aurelia): fine. please flag any maintenance so our SREs can coordinate.

[34:20] Liam (Redwood): will do.

[34:40] Marta (Aurelia): curious about instrumentation — what traces should we attach from our side to correlate?

[34:56] Sofia (Redwood): include request id, route tag, client-side timestamp, server receive timestamp, kernel selection flag, and cancel flag. that gives full causality for each microburst.

[35:30] Priya (Aurelia): sounds good. we'll wire that up.

[36:00] Liam (Redwood): one more thing — for the 10k test, we'll also send a baseline run with lowered batching window so you can compare cost and tail tradeoffs side by side.

[36:20] Carlos (Aurelia): perfect. do you have a preferred format for results? csv or dashboard link?

[36:35] Sofia (Redwood): CSV with percentiles plus a short pdf summary of findings and traces zipped. and a live dashboard link for canary.

[37:00] Priya (Aurelia): anything else on security? we need an updated SOC2 attestation for dedicated nodes.

[37:20] Liam (Redwood): we'll send the SOC2 addendum for Dedicated and the audit artifacts checklist.

[37:50] Carlos (Aurelia): appreciate it.

[38:10] (short silence)

[38:30] Liam (Redwood): ok final recap: sequence CSV -> Carlos by 2026-10-31; bench + traces -> Sofia by 2026-11-01; kernel spreadsheet -> Liam by 2026-11-01; canary rollout 2026-11-02 coordinated by Priya/Evan. and we will set up a 30-min readout after results.

[39:20] Liam (Redwood): yes penciled. we'll confirm in calendar.

[39:55] Evan (Aurelia): none from SRE beyond what we said.
